leadIn:
I’m using the active Settle workflow: I’ll first inspect the renaming flow, its tests, and repository guidance, then bring only genuinely user-owned behavior choices to the native question form before changing code.

The initial repository scan is still returning, so I’m letting that read-only pass finish before narrowing into the owning module and tests.

This is a **bounded** change: the existing single-directory rename flow owns the behavior in `src/rename.js`; no new API, persistent format, or subsystem is required.

Verified facts:

- `applyRenames` performs synchronous renames one by one, so any later error leaves earlier steps applied (`src/rename.js`, `applyRenames`).
- The CLI prints the entire plan before applying it and currently has no error handling (`src/cli.js`).
- The documented complaint is specifically an `EEXIST` collision leaving a partial run, while undo/journaling is explicitly out of scope (`README.md`, “Known rough edge” and “Out of scope”).
- Runs are scripted and are often accidentally repeated (`README.md`, “How it is used”).

**Inference:** preflight validation is the natural seam, but repository evidence does not decide whether conflicts should abort, be skipped, or replace files, nor what guarantee applies if the directory changes after validation.

What waits on these answers: the externally visible collision contract, repeated-run behavior, and whether execution must compensate for a mid-run change.

questions.question: When any planned target is already occupied, what should the whole run do? A wrong choice can either preserve unwanted files, destroy them, or produce only part of the requested result. Evidence: `src/rename.js` currently stops on the first rename error; `README.md` identifies the resulting partial run as the complaint.

options.label: Abort unchanged (Recommended)
options.description: Validate the full plan and rename nothing; safest, but the user must resolve every conflict before retrying.

options.label: Skip conflicts
options.description: Rename non-conflicting files and report skipped ones; completes useful work, but intentionally permits partial results.

options.label: Replace targets
options.description: Overwrite conflicting targets and finish; convenient, but can irreversibly destroy unrelated files.

questions.question: If another renamer instance or script changes a valid source or target after validation but before this run finishes, what should this run guarantee? A wrong choice can reintroduce partial results under concurrent use. Evidence: `README.md` says the command is script-driven and may be invoked twice; `applyRenames` has no coordination.

options.label: Rollback and fail (Recommended)
options.description: Attempt to restore this run’s completed steps and report failure; protects all-or-nothing behavior, but rollback itself can fail after hostile external changes.

options.label: Leave and fail
options.description: Stop at the filesystem error and retain completed steps; simplest, but partial runs remain possible under concurrency.

options.label: Refuse overlap
options.description: Reject an overlapping invocation using coordination; clearer concurrency behavior, but adds lock lifecycle and stale-lock recovery.

questions.question: May a target name be occupied initially by another source in the same rename plan? A wrong choice can reject valid reorderings or overwrite data during chains/cycles. Evidence: `planRenames` derives targets without checking whether those names are also matched sources (`src/rename.js`).

options.label: Support plan moves (Recommended)
options.description: Treat matched sources as movable and safely handle chains/cycles; more complete, but requires temporary staging.

options.label: Abort as conflict
options.description: Require every target to be initially free unless it is the same file; simpler, but rejects some otherwise valid bulk renames.

leadIn:
The first round settles three user-owned points: any external collision aborts before changes; sources participating in the same plan may move through occupied names; and a failure after execution begins triggers rollback and failure.

Further inspection of the generated plan exposes the next frontier:

- A replacement without `#` assigns every match the same target (`src/rename.js`, `replacement.replace`), so duplicate destinations can exist before touching disk.
- A repeated run can generate identity steps such as `photo-001.jpg -> photo-001.jpg`; accidental repetition is documented as common (`README.md`).
- The CLI currently writes every proposed step to stdout before execution, while uncaught filesystem errors become diagnostics and a nonzero process exit (`src/cli.js`).
- Staging is required by the chosen support for plan-internal moves; no persistent journal is allowed (`README.md`, “Out of scope”).

**Open tension:** identity steps are harmless, but duplicate destinations cannot all succeed; and printing “A -> B” before an aborted run may falsely look like success to scripts.

What waits on these answers: validation rules and the stable stdout/failure contract.

questions.question: When multiple sources map to the same target, what should happen? A wrong choice can silently discard files or make ordering decide the winner. Evidence: `planRenames` permits this when the replacement omits `#` (`src/rename.js`).

options.label: Abort unchanged (Recommended)
options.description: Report the duplicate target and touch nothing; preserves every source, but rejects single-name replacements over multiple matches.

options.label: Keep first
options.description: Rename only the first source and skip the rest; deterministic, but deliberately produces a partial plan.

questions.question: When a source already has exactly its planned target name, how should that step behave? A wrong choice can make accidental reruns fail unnecessarily or conceal other real conflicts. Evidence: reruns are common (`README.md`) and `planRenames` can produce `from === to` (`src/rename.js`).

options.label: No-op step (Recommended)
options.description: Accept identical source/target as already complete while still validating all other steps; friendly to reruns, but does not announce that the file was unchanged.

options.label: Abort run
options.description: Treat an identity step as a conflict and change nothing; strict, but makes already-correct reruns fail.

questions.question: When validation or execution fails, what should stdout contain? A wrong choice affects scripts that may interpret printed mappings as completed work. Evidence: `src/cli.js` currently prints the whole plan before applying it, and repository conventions reserve stderr for diagnostics.

options.label: Only completed (Recommended)
options.description: Write mappings to stdout only after the full run succeeds, and put the failure on stderr with nonzero exit; unambiguous, but removes advance progress output.

options.label: Keep proposed plan
options.description: Print mappings before attempting work and report failure on stderr; preserves current output timing, but stdout can describe changes that never happened.

leadIn:
The second round settles duplicate destinations as a preflight abort, identity steps as no-ops, and stdout as a record of a fully successful run only.

Two material edges remain:

- `replacement` is joined directly to the chosen directory, so values containing separators or `..` can currently address paths outside that directory (`src/rename.js`, `path.join`).
- The chosen rollback guarantee can be defeated by an external writer; without a journal, the only recoverable evidence may be staged files in the working directory (`README.md` excludes persistent rename journals).
- Missing/unreadable directories fail during `matchFiles` before mutation (`src/match.js`); a source disappearing later is the already-settled mid-run failure case.
- The package is private and the only in-repository consumers of the plan shape are `src/cli.js` and `test/rename.test.js` (`package.json`, imports).

**Open tension:** tightening path containment improves safety but changes accepted input, while deleting staged evidence after a failed rollback would make recovery impossible.

What waits on these answers: the trust boundary for generated names and the exact state left after an unsuccessful rollback.

questions.question: Must every generated target remain a plain filename inside the selected directory? A wrong choice either preserves a potentially relied-on cross-directory behavior or allows a replacement to escape the tool’s documented single-directory boundary. Evidence: `README.md` says renaming is within one directory, but `src/rename.js` currently accepts separators and `..`.

options.label: Stay in directory (Recommended)
options.description: Reject absolute, nested, `.` and `..` targets before mutation; enforces the documented boundary, but tightens compatibility for users moving files via replacement.

options.label: Preserve path input
options.description: Continue allowing joined relative paths; avoids a compatibility change, but permits writes outside the documented directory.

questions.question: If rollback itself cannot restore every source because another process changed the paths, what should remain? A wrong choice can erase the last recoverable copy or leave surprising artifacts. Evidence: the selected behavior requires rollback, while `README.md` rules out a persistent journal.

options.label: Keep staged files (Recommended)
options.description: Preserve uniquely marked files and report each location on stderr; maximizes manual recovery, but leaves cleanup to the user.

options.label: Remove staging
options.description: Clean temporary names even after rollback trouble; leaves a tidier directory, but may destroy recoverable content.

leadIn:
The frontier is now closed. Repository evidence also settles the remaining probes: empty matches already form an empty successful plan (`matchFiles` + `planRenames`); recursive work and undo are explicitly excluded (`README.md`); plan objects stay `{from,to}` for the CLI/test consumers; state is temporary within the selected directory and exists only during a run; there is no data migration or remote authorization boundary; CLI argument failures remain pre-mutation diagnostics.

User-settled ledger lines:

- External occupied target → abort unchanged.
- Duplicate planned target → abort unchanged.
- Concurrent valid change after validation → rollback completed work and fail.
- Plan-internal occupied source → support chains/cycles through staging.
- Partial execution failure → rollback and fail.
- Repeated identity step → accept as a no-op.
- Failure output → stdout only after complete success; diagnostics on stderr with nonzero exit.
- Target validation → plain filenames confined to the selected directory.
- Rollback failure residue → retain uniquely staged recoverable files and report their locations.

**Resolved contract:** validate the complete plan before mutation; perform collision-safe staged renames; on execution failure, restore the starting names where possible; never overwrite an unrelated target; print mappings only after success. Excluded: recursion, undo/journaling, and cross-directory targets. Focused tests plus `node --test` will prove unchanged-on-conflict, duplicate rejection, identity reruns, plan moves, containment, successful output, and rollback behavior.

What waits on confirmation: implementation, executable verification, and the required decision record.

questions.question: Does this resolved contract capture the fix, or is anything missing or wrong? Confirming authorizes implementation and verification exactly within these boundaries.

options.label: Implement it (Recommended)
options.description: Build and test the settled all-or-nothing behavior; limitation: rollback remains best-effort against hostile concurrent filesystem changes.

options.label: Revise contract
options.description: Pause implementation so you can change a settled behavior through the free-form response; delays the fix but avoids encoding the wrong contract.
